theory.intro: Because $\sin\theta=\sin(180^{\circ}-\theta)$, an acute angle and its obtuse partner share the same sine. When the sine value is strictly between $0$ and $1$, the calculator's $\sin^{-1}$ returns the acute angle, so the obtuse angle is $180^{\circ}-\theta$. Decide from the diagram or the wording which one the triangle needs.
facts: $\sin\theta=\sin(180^{\circ}-\theta)$, so an acute angle and its obtuse partner have exactly the same sine.
For a sine value strictly between $0$ and $1$, the calculator's $\sin^{-1}$ key returns the acute angle. When the sine is $1$, it returns $90^{\circ}$, whose supplementary angle is also $90^{\circ}$.
Subtract the calculator's value from $180^{\circ}$ to get the obtuse solution.
The largest angle of a triangle lies opposite the longest side, so only that angle can be obtuse.
If the side opposite the unknown angle is shorter than the side opposite the known angle, the unknown angle must be acute.
A triangle cannot have two obtuse angles, so a given obtuse angle rules out a second one.
Keep the full calculator value in the working and round only on the last line.
steps: Write the sine rule with sin on top
Substitute the known angle and the two sides
Make sin of the unknown angle the subject
For a sine value strictly between 0 and 1, take the inverse sine to get the acute angle
Decide whether the triangle needs the acute angle, the obtuse angle, or both
Subtract the acute angle from 180 degrees for the obtuse solution

workedExamples.solution_text:
$\theta$ is opposite the $12$ cm side; $28^{\circ}$ is opposite the $8$ cm side.
$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\theta}{12}&=\frac{\sin28^{\circ}}{8}\\ \sin\theta&=\frac{12\sin28^{\circ}}{8}\end{align*}$
The calculator gives the acute angle.
$\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{12\sin28^{\circ}}{8}\right)=44.765542\ldots^{\circ}$
Since $\theta$ is obtuse, subtract the unrounded acute angle from $180^{\circ}$.
$\begin{align*}\theta&=180^{\circ}-44.765542\ldots^{\circ}\\ \theta&\approx135^{\circ}\end{align*}$

The angles opposite the $15$ cm side are $\angle AQC$ and $\angle APC$. Each has the same sine.
$\begin{align*}\frac{\sin\theta}{15}&=\frac{\sin24^{\circ}}{9}\\ \sin\theta&=\frac{15\sin24^{\circ}}{9}\end{align*}$
The acute angle is at $Q$.
$\begin{align*}\angle AQC&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{15\sin24^{\circ}}{9}\right)\\ \angle AQC&=42.679322\ldots^{\circ}\\ \angle AQC&\approx43^{\circ}\end{align*}$
The obtuse angle at $P$ is its supplementary angle.
$\begin{align*}\angle APC&=180^{\circ}-42.679322\ldots^{\circ}\\ \angle APC&\approx137^{\circ}\end{align*}$
Both triangles are valid: $24^{\circ}+42.679322\ldots^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$ and $24^{\circ}+137.320677\ldots^{\circ}<180^{\circ}$.

development.question_text:
In triangle $PQR$, $PR=52$ cm, $QR=38$ cm and $\angle QPR=33^{\circ}$.
Find obtuse $\angle PQR$, to the nearest degree.
development.solution_text:
$\angle PQR$ is opposite the $52$ cm side and $33^{\circ}$ is opposite the $38$ cm side.
$\dfrac{\sin\angle PQR}{52}=\dfrac{\sin 33^{\circ}}{38}$
$\sin\angle PQR=\dfrac{52\sin 33^{\circ}}{38}$
$=0.745295\ldots$
The inverse sine gives the acute angle $48.184488\ldots^{\circ}$, and $\angle PQR$ is obtuse.
$\angle PQR=180^{\circ}-\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{52\sin 33^{\circ}}{38}\right)$
$\approx 132^{\circ}$
